techniques.name: GAN-Based Tabular Synthetic Data
techniques.description: Generates synthetic tabular datasets using Generative Adversarial Networks, most commonly through architectures such as CTGAN (Conditional Tabular GAN) and TVAE (Triplet-based Variational Autoencoder). These models learn the joint distribution of mixed-type columns — continuous, discrete, and categorical — by training a generator and discriminator in an adversarial framework, with mode-specific normalisation to handle multimodal continuous distributions and training-by-sampling to address class imbalance. The resulting synthetic tables aim to preserve statistical relationships, correlations, and marginal distributions of the original data whilst containing no real records, supporting privacy-preserving data sharing, model development on sensitive datasets, and augmentation of limited training data.

example_use_cases.description: Generating synthetic patient records from hospital databases using CTGAN to enable multi-institution collaborative research on treatment outcomes without sharing identifiable health data across organisational boundaries.

Augmenting a limited fraud detection training set by generating synthetic fraudulent transaction records that preserve the statistical characteristics of rare fraud patterns, improving model recall on underrepresented fraud types.

Creating balanced synthetic datasets for credit scoring by generating additional records for underrepresented demographic groups, enabling fairness testing across protected characteristics without collecting new sensitive data.

limitations.description: Training instability inherent to GAN architectures (mode collapse, vanishing gradients) can result in synthetic data that fails to capture the full diversity of the original distribution, particularly for rare categories or tail distributions.
Requires substantial computational resources and hyperparameter tuning, with training times scaling poorly for datasets with many columns or complex inter-column dependencies.

Privacy guarantees are not inherent — without additional mechanisms like differential privacy, GAN-generated data may leak information about training records through memorisation or membership inference attacks.
Performance degrades significantly on datasets with high cardinality categorical columns, complex temporal dependencies, or relational structures across multiple tables.

resources.title: Modeling Tabular data using Conditional GAN
resources.abstract: Modeling the probability distribution of rows in tabular data and generating realistic synthetic data is a non-trivial task. Tabular data usually contains a mix of discrete and continuous columns. Continuous columns may have multiple modes whereas discrete columns are sometimes imbalanced making the modeling difficult. Existing statistical and deep neural network models fail to properly model this type of data. We design TGAN, which uses a conditional generative adversarial network to address these challenges. To aid in a fair and thorough comparison, we design a benchmark with 7 simulated and 8 real datasets and several Bayesian network baselines. TGAN outperforms Bayesian methods on most of the real datasets whereas other deep learning methods could not.

A Review of Tabular Data Synthesis Using GANs on an IDS Dataset
resources.abstract: Recent technological innovations along with the vast amount of available data worldwide have led to the rise of cyberattacks against network systems. Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a crucial role as a defense mechanism in networks against adversarial attackers. Machine Learning methods provide various cybersecurity tools. However, these methods require plenty of data to be trained efficiently, which may be hard to collect or to use due to privacy reasons. One of the most notable Machine Learning tools is the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), and it has great potential for tabular data synthesis. In this work, we start by briefly presenting the most popular GAN architectures, VanillaGAN, WGAN, and WGAN-GP. Focusing on tabular data generation, CTGAN, CopulaGAN, and TableGAN models are used for the creation of synthetic IDS data. Specifically, the models are trained and evaluated on an NSL-KDD dataset, considering the limitations and requirements that this procedure needs. Finally, based on certain quantitative and qualitative methods, we argue and evaluate the most prominent GANs for tabular network data synthesis.

sample_claims.text: The synthetic patient dataset generated by CTGAN preserves statistical correlations between clinical variables whilst containing no records traceable to real patients
The augmented training dataset includes GAN-generated records for underrepresented demographic groups, achieving balanced representation across all protected characteristics
The fraud detection model has been validated on GAN-generated synthetic transaction data that preserves the statistical distribution of rare fraud patterns from the original dataset

techniques.name: Sequential CART Synthesis
techniques.description: Sequential CART synthesis creates an artificial copy of a confidential microdata set (records about individual people or organisations) that can be released in place of the real data, in the form used by the synthpop package for R. Variables are synthesised one at a time in a chosen order: the first is generated by sampling with replacement from its observed values, and for each later variable a classification or regression tree (CART) is fitted on the real data to predict it from the variables earlier in the order. Each synthetic record is passed down that tree using its already-synthesised values, and the new value is copied from a randomly chosen real record in the leaf it reaches, so the joint distribution of the data is rebuilt as a chain of conditional distributions. Disclosure risk is limited by setting a minimum leaf size, smoothing synthesised continuous values and removing synthetic records that reproduce unique real ones, and several synthetic copies can be released so that analysts can allow for the extra uncertainty that synthesis adds.

example_use_cases.description: A national longitudinal study that links census returns to administrative records such as births, deaths and cancer registrations for a sample of the population cannot let approved researchers take the data off site. Its support team runs CART synthesis to produce a bespoke synthetic extract for each project, so researchers can explore the data and write and test their analysis code at their own institution before the final model is run on the real data in the secure setting.

A hospital trust wants a university team to develop a readmission model without receiving patient records. It releases a CART-synthesised copy of the admissions table with a minimum leaf size of ten and kernel smoothing of continuous values, removes any synthetic record that matches a unique real patient on age, sex and postcode district, and runs a disclosure-risk assessment before release.

A national statistics office publishes a synthetic teaching file of its labour force survey for university courses, generated by sequential CART synthesis with the variable order and minimum leaf sizes chosen with subject experts, and labels every record as synthetic so that no reader mistakes a row for a real respondent.

limitations.description: It gives no formal privacy guarantee. No synthetic record is a real person, but trees can reproduce rare combinations and extreme values, and an intruder who knows that a real record holds the largest value of a variable can bound it from the synthetic maximum. Risk must be measured for each release and reduced with larger leaves, smoothing and removal of unique matches, each of which costs analytical value.

Relationships the trees miss disappear from the synthetic data. A tree grown from few records may never split on a variable that matters, so the synthetic data show no association where the real data have one; in the method's original evaluation a regression coefficient for sex was attenuated to zero in this way. Small subgroups and weak effects are the most exposed.

Results depend on the order in which variables are synthesised and on which earlier variables predict each later one. A careless order can produce impossible combinations, such as a detailed category that contradicts the summary variable derived from it, so detailed variables should be synthesised before derived ones and the output checked for inconsistencies.

Synthetic data cannot reproduce every analysis of the real data. Analyses the synthesiser did not plan for may give different answers, so a release should state which analyses it supports, and users should confirm key findings on the real data, for example through a verification service or secure access.

resources.title: synthpop: Bespoke Creation of Synthetic Data in R
resources.abstract: In many contexts, confidentiality constraints severely restrict access to unique and valuable microdata. Synthetic data which mimic the original observed data and preserve the relationships between variables but do not contain any disclosive records are one possible solution to this problem. The synthpop package for R, introduced in this paper, provides routines to generate synthetic versions of original data sets. We describe the methodology and its consequences for the data characteristics. We illustrate the package features using a survey data example.

resources.title: synthpop: Generating Synthetic Versions of Sensitive Microdata for Statistical Disclosure Control
resources.abstract: A tool for producing synthetic versions of microdata containing confidential information so that they are safe to be released to users for exploratory analysis. The key objective of generating synthetic data is to replace sensitive original values with synthetic ones causing minimal distortion of the statistical information contained in the data set. Variables, which can be categorical or continuous, are synthesised one-by-one using sequential modelling. Replacements are generated by drawing from conditional distributions fitted to the original data using parametric or classification and regression trees models. Data are synthesised via the function syn() which can be largely automated, if default settings are used, or with methods defined by the user. Optional parameters can be used to influence the disclosure risk and the analytical quality of the synthesised data. For a description of the implemented method see Nowok, Raab and Dibben (2016) <doi:10.18637/jss.v074.i11>. Functions to assess identity and attribute disclosure for the original and for the synthetic data are included in the package, and their use is illustrated in a vignette on disclosure (Practical Privacy Metrics for Synthetic Data).

resources.title: Using CART to Generate Partially Synthetic Public Use Microdata
resources.abstract: To limit disclosure risks, one approach is to release partially synthetic public use microdata sets. These comprise the units originally surveyed, but some collected values, for example sensitive values at high risk of disclosure or values of key identifiers, are replaced with multiple imputations. This article presents and evaluates the use of classification and regression trees to generate partially synthetic data. Two potential applications of CART are studied via simulation: (i) generate synthetic data for sensitive variables; and, (ii) generate synthetic data for variables that are key identifiers.

resources.title: Providing bespoke synthetic data for the UK Longitudinal Studies and other sensitive data with the synthpop package for R1
resources.abstract: Synthetic data methods were designed to address the conflicting demands placed on data holders to unlock the research and policy potential of microdata while at the same time preserving the confidentiality of individuals.Recently, these methods have become more widely recognized in the UK and the provision of bespoke synthetic data has been approved to expand the use of one of the UK Longitudinal Studies.The process of producing useful synthetic data involves, however, a substantial investment of research time, as it always requires some customising for the characteristics of an individual data set.At the same time, a substantial part of it can be automated and this is essential when the process has to be conducted rapidly and on a regular basis.This paper describes the application of synthetic data to the UK Longitudinal Studies, details implementation process for the Scottish Longitudinal Study and presents methods used in an R package synthpop that has been developed to facilitate production of non-disclosive entirely synthetic data.A reproducible example using open data is given to illustrate the synthesising procedure and to provide insights into quality of synthetic data generated using different automated approaches.

resources.abstract: What is synthpop? An R package for generating synthetic versions of sensitive microdata. A tool to create synthetic data and evaluate their utility.

sample_claims.text: The research extract released to the project team was generated by sequential CART synthesis with a minimum leaf size of ten and smoothing of continuous variables, and contains no record that reproduces a unique combination in the source data.

No confidential microdata left the secure environment during model development: external researchers wrote and tested their code on a synthetic extract, and only the final approved model was run on the real data.
A disclosure-risk assessment of the synthetic admissions table found no synthetic record matching a unique real patient on the agreed identifying variables.

techniques.name: Federated Learning
techniques.description: Federated learning enables collaborative model training across multiple distributed parties (devices, organisations, or data centres) without requiring centralised data sharing. Participants train models locally on their private datasets and only share model updates (gradients, weights, or aggregated statistics) with a central coordinator. This distributed approach serves multiple purposes: preserving data privacy and sovereignty, reducing communication costs, enabling learning from diverse data sources, improving model robustness through heterogeneous training, and facilitating compliance with data protection regulations whilst maintaining model performance comparable to centralised training.

example_use_cases.description: Developing a smartphone keyboard prediction model by learning from users' typing patterns without their text ever leaving their devices, enabling personalised predictions whilst maintaining complete data privacy.

Training a medical diagnosis model across multiple hospitals without sharing patient records, ensuring model robustness by learning from diverse patient populations and clinical practices across different institutions.

limitations.description: Communication overhead can be substantial, especially with frequent model updates and large models, potentially limiting scalability and increasing training time compared to centralised approaches.

Statistical heterogeneity across participants (non-IID data distributions) can lead to training instability, slower convergence, and reduced model performance compared to centralised training on pooled data.
System heterogeneity in computational capabilities, network connectivity, and availability of participating devices can create bottlenecks and introduce bias towards more capable participants.
Privacy vulnerabilities remain through gradient leakage attacks, model inversion, and membership inference attacks that can potentially reconstruct sensitive information from shared model updates.
Coordination complexity increases with the number of participants, requiring sophisticated aggregation protocols, fault tolerance mechanisms, and secure communication infrastructure.

resources.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data
resources.abstract: Modern mobile devices have access to a wealth of data suitable for learning models, which in turn can greatly improve the user experience on the device. For example, language models can improve speech recognition and text entry, and image models can automatically select good photos. However, this rich data is often privacy sensitive, large in quantity, or both, which may preclude logging to the data center and training there using conventional approaches. We advocate an alternative that leaves the training data distributed on the mobile devices, and learns a shared model by aggregating locally-computed updates. We term this decentralized approach Federated Learning. We present a practical method for the federated learning of deep networks based on iterative model averaging, and conduct an extensive empirical evaluation, considering five different model architectures and four datasets. These experiments demonstrate the approach is robust to the unbalanced and non-IID data distributions that are a defining characteristic of this setting. Communication costs are the principal constraint, and we show a reduction in required communication rounds by 10-100x as compared to synchronized stochastic gradient descent.

resources.title: Federated Learning - DeepLearning.AI
Federated learning for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19
resources.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a method used for training artificial intelligence models with data from multiple sources while maintaining data anonymity, thus removing many barriers to data sharing. Here we used data from 20 institutes across the globe to train a FL model, called EXAM (electronic medical record (EMR) chest X-ray AI model), that predicts the future oxygen requirements of symptomatic patients with COVID-19 using inputs of vital signs, laboratory data and chest X-rays. EXAM achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) >0.92 for predicting outcomes at 24 and 72 h from the time of initial presentation to the emergency room, and it provided 16% improvement in average AUC measured across all participating sites and an average increase in generalizability of 38% when compared with models trained at a single site using that site's data. For prediction of mechanical ventilation treatment or death at 24 h at the largest independent test site, EXAM achieved a sensitivity of 0.950 and specificity of 0.882. In this study, FL facilitated rapid data science collaboration without data exchange and generated a model that generalized across heterogeneous, unharmonized datasets for prediction of clinical outcomes in patients with COVID-19, setting the stage for the broader use of FL in healthcare.

resources.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
resources.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise across disciplines, out-of-sample generalizability is concerning. This is currently addressed by sharing multi-site data, but such centralization is challenging/infeasible to scale due to various limitations. Federated ML (FL) provides an alternative paradigm for accurate and generalizable ML, by only sharing numerical model updates. Here we present the largest FL study to-date, involving data from 71 sites across 6 continents, to generate an automatic tumor boundary detector for the rare disease of glioblastoma, reporting the largest such dataset in the literature ( n = 6, 314). We demonstrate a 33% delineation improvement for the surgically targetable tumor, and 23% for the complete tumor extent, over a publicly trained model. We anticipate our study to: 1) enable more healthcare studies informed by large diverse data, ensuring meaningful results for rare diseases and underrepresented populations, 2) facilitate further analyses for glioblastoma by releasing our consensus model, and 3) demonstrate the FL effectiveness at such scale and task-complexity as a paradigm shift for multi-site collaborations, alleviating the need for data-sharing.

sample_claims.text: The model training process does not require patient data to leave individual healthcare institutions
The diagnostic model performs reliably despite learning from patient populations with heterogeneous clinical characteristics across multiple sites
The keyboard prediction model learns from user typing patterns without transmitting personal text content to central servers

techniques.name: Differential Privacy
techniques.description: Differential privacy provides mathematically rigorous privacy protection by adding carefully calibrated random noise to data queries, statistical computations, or machine learning outputs. The technique works by ensuring that the presence or absence of any individual's data has minimal impact on the results - specifically, any query result should be nearly indistinguishable whether or not a particular person's data is included. This is achieved through controlled noise addition that scales with the query's sensitivity and a privacy budget (epsilon) that quantifies the privacy-utility trade-off. The smaller the epsilon, the more noise is added and the stronger the privacy guarantee, but at the cost of reduced accuracy.

example_use_cases.description: Protecting individual privacy in census data analysis by adding calibrated noise to demographic statistics, ensuring households cannot be re-identified whilst maintaining accurate population insights for policy planning.

Publishing differentially private aggregate statistics about model performance across different demographic groups, enabling transparent bias auditing without exposing sensitive individual prediction details or group membership.

limitations.description: Adding noise inherently reduces the accuracy and utility of results, with stronger privacy guarantees (smaller epsilon values) leading to more significant degradation in data quality.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.
Sequential queries consume the privacy budget cumulatively, potentially requiring careful query planning and potentially prohibiting future analyses once the budget is exhausted.
Implementation complexity is high, requiring deep understanding of sensitivity analysis, noise mechanisms, and composition theorems to avoid inadvertent privacy violations.
May not protect against all privacy attacks, particularly sophisticated adversaries with auxiliary information or when combined with other data sources that could aid re-identification.

resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
resources.abstract: The problem of privacy-preserving data analysis has a long history spanning multiple disciplines. As electronic data about individuals becomes increasingly detailed, and as technology enables ever more powerful collection and curation of these data, the need increases for a robust, meaningful, and mathematically rigorous definition of privacy, together with a computationally rich class of algorithms that satisfy this definition. Differential Privacy is such a definition. After motivating and discussing the meaning of differential privacy, the preponderance of this monograph is devoted to fundamental techniques for achieving differential privacy, and application of these techniques in creative combinations, using the query-release problem as an ongoing example. A key point is that, by rethinking the computational goal, one can often obtain far better results than would be achieved by methodically replacing each step of a non-private computation with a differentially private implementation. Despite some astonishingly powerful computational results, there are still fundamental limitations — not just on what can be achieved with differential privacy but on what can be achieved with any method that protects against a complete breakdown in privacy. Virtually all the algorithms discussed herein maintain differential privacy against adversaries of arbitrary computational power. Certain algorithms are computationally intensive, others are efficient. Computational complexity for the adversary and the algorithm are both discussed. We then turn from fundamentals to applications other than queryrelease, discussing differentially private methods for mechanism design and machine learning. The vast majority of the literature on differentially private algorithms considers a single, static, database that is subject to many analyses. Differential privacy in other models, including distributed databases and computations on data streams is discussed. Finally, we note that this work is meant as a thorough introduction to the problems and techniques of differential privacy, but is not intended to be an exhaustive survey — there is by now a vast amount of work in differential privacy, and we can cover only a small portion of it.

The 2020 Census Disclosure Avoidance System TopDown Algorithm
resources.abstract: The Census TopDown Algorithm (TDA) is a disclosure avoidance system using differential privacy for privacy-loss accounting.The algorithm ingests the final, edited version of the 2020 Census data and the final tabulation geographic definitions.The algorithm then creates noisy versions of key queries on the data, referred to as measurements, using zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy.Another key aspect of the TDA are invariants, statistics that the Census Bureau has determined, as matter of policy, to exclude from the privacyloss accounting.The TDA postprocesses the measurements together with the invariants to produce a Microdata Detail File (MDF) that contains one record for each person and one record for each housing unit enumerated in the 2020 Census.The MDF is passed to the 2020 Census tabulation system to produce the 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File.This article describes the mathematics and testing of the TDA for this purpose.

resources.title: RAPPOR
resources.abstract: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response, or RAPPOR, is a technology for crowdsourcing statistics from end-user client software, anonymously, with strong privacy guarantees. In short, RAPPORs allow the forest of client data to be studied, without permitting the possibility of looking at individual trees. By applying randomized response in a novel manner, RAPPOR provides the mechanisms for such collection as well as for efficient, high-utility analysis of the collected data. In particular, RAPPOR permits statistics to be collected on the population of client-side strings with strong privacy guarantees for each client, and without linkability of their reports. This paper describes and motivates RAPPOR, details its differential-privacy and utility guarantees, discusses its practical deployment and properties in the face of different attack models, and, finally, gives results of its application to both synthetic and real-world data.

sample_claims.text: The census data analysis results remain statistically indistinguishable whether any single household's data is included or excluded
The medical research system's published statistics provide quantified privacy guarantees that bound the maximum disclosure risk for any individual patient
The model performance metrics across demographic groups are accompanied by documented privacy budget allocation and noise parameters
The system's privacy protection level is mathematically bounded and remains effective even under repeated queries within the allocated budget

techniques.name: Machine Unlearning
techniques.description: Machine unlearning enables removal of specific training data's influence from trained models without complete retraining. This technique addresses privacy rights like GDPR's right to be forgotten by selectively erasing learned patterns associated with particular data points, individuals, or sensitive attributes. Methods include exact unlearning (provably equivalent to retraining without the data), approximate unlearning (efficient algorithms that closely approximate retraining), and certified unlearning (providing formal guarantees about information removal).

example_use_cases.description: Responding to user deletion requests in a social media recommendation system by removing all influence of that user's historical interactions, ensuring GDPR compliance and verifiable data removal.

Enabling a financial institution to demonstrate regulatory compliance by providing cryptographic proof that a former customer's transaction history has been completely removed from credit risk assessment models following account closure.

limitations.description: Exact unlearning for complex models like deep neural networks is computationally expensive, often nearly as costly as full retraining.
Approximate unlearning methods may not provide strong guarantees that information has been fully removed, potentially leaving residual influence.
Difficult to verify unlearning effectiveness, as adversaries might extract information about supposedly removed data through membership inference or other attacks.
Repeated unlearning requests can degrade model performance significantly, especially if many data points are removed from the training distribution.
Requires access to model architecture and training process details (white-box access), making it difficult to apply to third-party models or models where internal structure is proprietary.
Particularly challenging for very large foundation models where even storing checkpoints for potential retraining is infeasible, limiting practical applicability to smaller, domain-specific models.

resources.title: Digital forgetting in large language models: A survey of unlearning methods
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the state of the art in natural language processing. The massive adoption of generative LLMs and the capabilities they have shown have prompted public concerns regarding their impact on the labor market, privacy, the use of copyrighted work, and how these models align with human ethics and the rule of law. As a response, new regulations are being pushed, which require developers and service providers to evaluate, monitor, and forestall or at least mitigate the risks posed by their models. One mitigation strategy is digital forgetting: given a model with undesirable knowledge or behavior, the goal is to obtain a new model where the detected issues are no longer present. Digital forgetting is usually enforced via machine unlearning techniques, which modify trained machine learning models for them to behave as models trained on a subset of the original training data. In this work, we describe the motivations and desirable properties of digital forgetting when applied to LLMs, and we survey recent works on machine unlearning. Specifically, we propose a taxonomy of unlearning methods based on the reach and depth of the modifications done on the models, we discuss and compare the effectiveness of machine unlearning methods for LLMs proposed so far, and we survey their evaluation. Finally, we describe open problems of machine unlearning applied to LLMs and we put forward recommendations for developers and practitioners.

resources.title: Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Today's systems produce a rapidly exploding amount of data, and the data further derives more data, forming a complex data propagation network that we call the data's lineage. There are many reasons that users want systems to forget certain data including its lineage. From a privacy perspective, users who become concerned with new privacy risks of a system often want the system to forget their data and lineage. From a security perspective, if an attacker pollutes an anomaly detector by injecting manually crafted data into the training data set, the detector must forget the injected data to regain security. From a usability perspective, a user can remove noise and incorrect entries so that a recommendation engine gives useful recommendations. Therefore, we envision forgetting systems, capable of forgetting certain data and their lineages, completely and quickly. This paper focuses on making learning systems forget, the process of which we call machine unlearning, or simply unlearning. We present a general, efficient unlearning approach by transforming learning algorithms used by a system into a summation form. To forget a training data sample, our approach simply updates a small number of summations -- asymptotically faster than retraining from scratch. Our approach is general, because the summation form is from the statistical query learning in which many machine learning algorithms can be implemented. Our approach also applies to all stages of machine learning, including feature selection and modeling. Our evaluation, on four diverse learning systems and real-world workloads, shows that our approach is general, effective, fast, and easy to use.

resources.title: Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Once users have shared their data online, it is generally difficult for them to revoke access and ask for the data to be deleted. Machine learning (ML) exacerbates this problem because any model trained with said data may have memorized it, putting users at risk of a successful privacy attack exposing their information. Yet, having models unlearn is notoriously difficult.We introduce SISA training, a framework that expedites the unlearning process by strategically limiting the influence of a data point in the training procedure. While our framework is applicable to any learning algorithm, it is designed to achieve the largest improvements for stateful algorithms like stochastic gradient descent for deep neural networks. SISA training reduces the computational overhead associated with unlearning, even in the worst-case setting where unlearning requests are made uniformly across the training set. In some cases, the service provider may have a prior on the distribution of unlearning requests that will be issued by users. We may take this prior into account to partition and order data accordingly, and further decrease overhead from unlearning.Our evaluation spans several datasets from different domains, with corresponding motivations for unlearning. Under no distributional assumptions, for simple learning tasks, we observe that SISA training improves time to unlearn points from the Purchase dataset by 4.63×, and 2.45× for the SVHN dataset, over retraining from scratch. SISA training also provides a speed-up of 1.36× in retraining for complex learning tasks such as ImageNet classification; aided by transfer learning, this results in a small degradation in accuracy. Our work contributes to practical data governance in machine unlearning.

resources.title: Recommendation Unlearning
resources.abstract: Recommender systems provide essential web services by learning users’ personal preferences from collected data. However, in many cases, systems also need to forget some training data. From the perspective of privacy, users desire a tool to erase the impacts of their sensitive data from the trained models. From the perspective of utility, if a system’s utility is damaged by some bad data, the system needs to forget such data to regain utility. While unlearning is very important, it has not been well-considered in existing recommender systems. Although there are some researches have studied the problem of machine unlearning, existing methods can not be directly applied to recommendation as they are unable to consider the collaborative information.

techniques.name: Membership Inference Attack Testing
techniques.description: Membership inference attack testing evaluates whether adversaries can determine if specific data points were included in a model's training set. This technique simulates attacks where adversaries use model confidence scores, prediction patterns, or loss values to distinguish training data from non-training data. Testing measures privacy leakage by calculating attack success rates, precision-recall trade-offs, and advantage over random guessing. Results inform decisions about privacy-enhancing techniques like differential privacy or regularisation.

example_use_cases.description: Testing a genomics research model to ensure attackers cannot determine which individuals' genetic data were used in training, protecting highly sensitive hereditary and health information from privacy breaches.
Evaluating whether a facial recognition system leaks information about whose faces were in the training set, preventing unauthorized identification of individuals in training data.

Auditing a credit scoring model used by multiple lenders to verify and transparently document that the model doesn't leak information about which specific customers' financial histories were used in training, supporting fair lending compliance reporting.

limitations.description: Attack success rates vary significantly depending on model architecture, training procedures, and data characteristics, making it difficult to establish universal thresholds for acceptable privacy.
Sophisticated attackers with shadow models or auxiliary data may achieve attack success rates 2-3x higher than standard evaluation scenarios test.
Trade-off between model utility and privacy protection means defending against membership inference often reduces model accuracy.
Testing requires access to both training and non-training data from the same distribution, which may not always be available for realistic evaluation.

resources.title: SoK: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs are Rushing Nowhere (and How to Fix It)
resources.abstract: Whether Large Language models (LLMs) memorize their training data and what this means, from measuring privacy leakage to detecting copyright violations, has become a rapidly growing area of research. In the last few months, more than 10 new methods have been proposed to perform Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) against LLMs. Contrary to traditional MIAs which rely on fixed-but randomized-records or models, these methods are mostly trained and tested on datasets collected post-hoc. Sets of members and non-members, used to evaluate the MIA, are constructed using informed guesses after the release of a model. This lack of randomization raises concerns of a distribution shift between members and non-members. In this work, we first extensively review the literature on MIAs against LLMs and show that, while most work focuses on sequence-level MIAs evaluated in post-hoc setups, a range of target models, motivations and units of interest are considered. We then quantify distribution shifts present in 6 datasets used in the literature, ranging from books to papers using a model-less bag of word classifier and compare the model-less results to the MIA. Our analysis shows that all of these datasets constructed post-hoc suffer from strong distribution shifts. These shifts invalidate the claims of LLMs memorizing strongly in real-world scenarios and, potentially, also the methodological contributions of the recent papers based on these datasets. Yet, all hope might not be lost. In the second part of this work, we introduce important considerations to properly evaluate MIAs against LLMs and discuss, in turn, potential ways forwards: randomized test splits, injections of randomized (unique) sequences, randomized finetuning, and several post-hoc control methods. While each option comes with its advantages and limitations, we believe they collectively provide solid grounds to guide the development of MIA methods and study LLM memorization. We conclude with an overview of recommended approaches to benchmark sequence-level and document-level MIAs against LLMs.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: We quantitatively investigate how machine learning models leak information about the individual data records on which they were trained. We focus on the basic membership inference attack: given a data record and black-box access to a model, determine if the record was in the model's training dataset. To perform membership inference against a target model, we make adversarial use of machine learning and train our own inference model to recognize differences in the target model's predictions on the inputs that it trained on versus the inputs that it did not train on. We empirically evaluate our inference techniques on classification models trained by commercial "machine learning as a service" providers such as Google and Amazon. Using realistic datasets and classification tasks, including a hospital discharge dataset whose membership is sensitive from the privacy perspective, we show that these models can be vulnerable to membership inference attacks. We then investigate the factors that influence this leakage and evaluate mitigation strategies.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
resources.abstract: A membership inference attack allows an adversary to query a trained machine learning model to predict whether or not a particular example was contained in the model’s training dataset. These attacks are currently evaluated using average-case “accuracy” metrics that fail to characterize whether the attack can confidently identify any members of the training set. We argue that attacks should instead be evaluated by computing their true-positive rate at low (e.g., ≤ 0.1%) false-positive rates, and find most prior attacks perform poorly when evaluated in this way. To address this we develop a Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) that carefully combines multiple ideas from the literature. Our attack is 10× more powerful at low false-positive rates, and also strictly dominates prior attacks on existing metrics.

Privacy Risks from Genomic Data-Sharing Beacons
resources.abstract: The human genetics community needs robust protocols that enable secure sharing of genomic data from participants in genetic research. Beacons are web servers that answer allele-presence queries--such as "Do you have a genome that has a specific nucleotide (e.g., A) at a specific genomic position (e.g., position 11,272 on chromosome 1)?"--with either "yes" or "no." Here, we show that individuals in a beacon are susceptible to re-identification even if the only data shared include presence or absence information about alleles in a beacon. Specifically, we propose a likelihood-ratio test of whether a given individual is present in a given genetic beacon. Our test is not dependent on allele frequencies and is the most powerful test for a specified false-positive rate. Through simulations, we showed that in a beacon with 1,000 individuals, re-identification is possible with just 5,000 queries. Relatives can also be identified in the beacon. Re-identification is possible even in the presence of sequencing errors and variant-calling differences. In a beacon constructed with 65 European individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project, we demonstrated that it is possible to detect membership in the beacon with just 250 SNPs. With just 1,000 SNP queries, we were able to detect the presence of an individual genome from the Personal Genome Project in an existing beacon. Our results show that beacons can disclose membership and implied phenotypic information about participants and do not protect privacy a priori. We discuss risk mitigation through policies and standards such as not allowing anonymous pings of genetic beacons and requiring minimum beacon sizes.

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation checks whether an artificial dataset made to stand in for sensitive real records is safe to share and still useful, and reports the trade-off between the two. Privacy is tested by simulating an attacker who holds the synthetic data and some facts about a person, and measuring how accurately the attacker can use the data to infer that person's sensitive values. Fidelity is tested by comparing the synthetic and real data column by column and in pairs of columns. Another check trains a classifier to tell the two apart, and a classifier that cannot beat chance suggests they are statistically alike. Utility is tested by running the analyses or training the models the data is meant for on the synthetic data and comparing the results with those from the real data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research office wants to share synthetic outpatient records with university partners. Before release it simulates an attacker who knows each patient's age band, sex and postcode district and tries to infer their diagnosis from the synthetic table, and it withholds the data if the attack does better than guessing from overall diagnosis rates.

A national statistics office gives researchers synthetic microdata for exploratory analysis. After the researchers settle on their models, the office runs the same models on the real data inside a secure environment and compares the estimates, to tell the researchers whether their exploratory conclusions can be trusted.

A bank's fraud team generates synthetic card transactions to share with an external vendor. It compares how often each fraud type appears and how amount, merchant type and time of day relate in the real and synthetic data, then checks that a model trained on the synthetic data still catches rare fraud in held-out real transactions.

limitations.description: Stronger privacy protection usually costs data quality, so the three scores pull against each other. There is no neutral threshold: where to set the balance depends on how sensitive the data is and what it will be used for, and the evaluation reports the trade-off without settling it.

Attack-based privacy tests only probe the attacks and attacker knowledge that were tried. A dataset that resists them may still leak to an attacker with more auxiliary information or a better method, so a good result is not proof of safety.

Fidelity and utility scores depend on which metrics, models and analyses are chosen. A synthetic dataset can match the real data on the columns and column pairs checked yet differ in ways that matter for a particular analysis, and general and analysis-specific utility scores can disagree.

Scores summarise the whole table, so rare events and small subgroups can be lost without moving the totals much. A fraud pattern or a minority group that the generator has smoothed away may show up only if the evaluation is designed to look for it.

The tests need statistical, privacy-engineering and domain expertise to set up and read. A classifier-based fidelity check can be misled by over-fitting or under-fitting the classifier, and weak settings can make poor synthetic data look good.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

resources.title: Quality Report | SDMetrics
A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

resources.abstract: We investigate whether Differentially Private SGD offers better privacy in practice than what is guaranteed by its state-of-the-art analysis. We do so via novel data poisoning attacks, which we show correspond to realistic privacy attacks. While previous work (Ma et al., arXiv 2019) proposed this connection between differential privacy and data poisoning as a defense against data poisoning, our use as a tool for understanding the privacy of a specific mechanism is new. More generally, our work takes a quantitative, empirical approach to understanding the privacy afforded by specific implementations of differentially private algorithms that we believe has the potential to complement and influence analytical work on differential privacy.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: Attacker-Model Re-identification Risk Measurement
techniques.description: Attacker-model re-identification risk measurement estimates, for a table of real records about people that is about to be released or shared, the probability that an attacker who links it with other information could correctly match a record to the person it describes. This record follows the attacker models of El Emam and Dankar (prosecutor and journalist) and of Dankar and El Emam (marketer), as implemented in the ARX tool: the assessor lists the quasi-identifiers (columns such as age, sex, postcode and admission date that an attacker could know or find), groups the records that share the same values on them, and names the attacker being guarded against. For a prosecutor, who knows the target is in the table, a record's risk is one over the size of its group in the table; for a journalist, who does not know this and links to a register of the wider population, it is one over the size of the matching group in that population, estimated with a statistical model when the population counts are not known; for a marketer, who tries to match as many records as possible, the measure is the expected share of records matched correctly. The assessor reports the highest record risk, the average risk and the share of records above a threshold set for the release, which decides whether the table can go out as it is or needs more generalisation or suppression first. It measures how easily records can be matched to people under the stated assumptions, unlike k-anonymity, which transforms the data, and it does not measure what can be learned about someone from values their whole group shares.

example_use_cases.description: A health insurer releasing claims data for a public prediction competition assumes an attacker who knows a neighbour's age, sex and a few of their claims, and measures each record's risk as one over the size of its group among all the insurer's members. It generalises ages and procedure codes until the measured probability of re-identification is below the 0.05 threshold agreed for the release, then checks the result with simulated matching attacks.

A pharmaceutical company sharing participant-level data from a completed trial with external researchers measures risk against the wider population, not the trial sample, because the participants are a small sample of everyone with the condition. It estimates how many records are unique in that population with ARX's uniqueness models and records the quasi-identifiers, attacker model, estimator and threshold in the data-sharing agreement for the researchers' data access committee to review.

A city transport authority planning to give a commuting dataset of home district, work district, age band and usual travel times to a contractor training a demand-forecasting model runs the assessment, finds a large share of records unique on home and work district together, merges small districts before sharing, and re-runs the assessment to confirm that the share of records above its threshold has fallen below the agreed limit.

limitations.description: The numbers are only as good as the list of quasi-identifiers and the attacker model behind them. A column left off the list, or an attacker who knows more (several of a person's hospital visits rather than one), can make records far easier to match than the assessment reports, and the assessor has to guess what other data an attacker holds. Repeating the assessment for stronger attackers, as some releases do with simulated matching, shows how sensitive the result is to these guesses.

It measures the chance of finding which record is a person's, not what can be learned about them. If all 20 records in a group share the same diagnosis, each has a measured risk of 1 in 20, yet anyone known to belong to the group has their diagnosis disclosed. Checks on the sensitive values, such as l-diversity, are needed alongside it when the release contains sensitive columns.

The journalist measure needs to know how common each record's values are in the wider population, which is rarely known and is estimated from the sample with statistical models; an evaluation of four estimators of population uniqueness on six clinical datasets found none accurate in all conditions. A small sample does not make re-identification unlikely in itself: one study estimated that 15 demographic attributes would let 99.98 per cent of Americans be correctly re-identified in any dataset.

There is no universal threshold, and the measure chosen changes the answer. For the same records the prosecutor measure is always at least as high as the journalist measure, so applying it to a release that is a small sample of a population over-protects and strips detail the data's users need; El Emam and Dankar found this effect strongest at small sampling fractions. The threshold, and which measure it applies to, must be justified for each release.

It measures one table as released, at one time. An attacker can combine several releases of the same data, or successive versions of a table that is updated, and longitudinal data, where each person has many events, need the attacker's knowledge of several events to be modelled explicitly. The basic measures do neither, so each additional or updated release needs its own assessment that takes the earlier ones into account.

techniques.name: Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
techniques.description: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains a neural network, or another model fitted by gradient descent, so that the finished model carries a formal differential privacy guarantee about the individual examples it was trained on. Differential privacy is more often applied by adding calibrated noise to the answer of a query or to a published statistic; DP-SGD instead changes the training algorithm itself. At each step it draws a random batch, computes the gradient (the direction in which an example pushes the model's parameters) separately for every example, scales down any gradient longer than a fixed clipping bound, adds Gaussian noise proportional to that bound to the sum, and updates the model with the noisy average, so that no single example can move the model by much and what influence remains is masked. A privacy accountant adds up the privacy cost of every step from the noise level, the sampling rate and the number of steps, and reports the total as epsilon and delta: epsilon limits how much more likely any trained model is with a given example in the training data than without it, and delta is a small probability that this limit fails. The output is a trained model with a stated (epsilon, delta) guarantee, which also covers anything later computed from the model, including its predictions.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank wants to give a credit-default model to a partner lender, which will hold the model weights. Its data science team trains the model with DP-SGD in Opacus, with each customer contributing one training example so that the guarantee protects a customer, targets epsilon 2 at a delta below one over the number of customers, and records the noise multiplier, clipping bound, sampling rate and accountant output in the model's release file.

A consortium of hospitals publishes the weights of a chest X-ray classifier so that other hospitals can fine-tune it locally. It trains with DP-SGD using one image per patient, replaces the network's batch normalisation layers with group normalisation as Opacus requires, and publishes the (epsilon, delta) guarantee and its unit, one patient, with the weights so that receiving hospitals can cite it in their own assessments.

A recruitment platform fine-tunes a language model, pretrained on public text, on job applicants' CVs (one per applicant) to suggest skills tags. It fine-tunes with DP-SGD, adds the cost of the hyperparameter search it ran on the CVs to the privacy budget, and compares tagging accuracy with a non-private fine-tune to decide whether the accuracy cost at its chosen epsilon is acceptable.

limitations.description: Clipping and noise reduce accuracy, and the reduction is not shared evenly: classes and groups that are rare in the training data lose the most, so a private model can widen an existing accuracy gap between groups. In the original experiments the drop at epsilon 8 was about 1 percentage point on handwritten digits but about 7 on a harder ten-class image task. Accuracy should be reported per group, and pretraining on public data or more training data is often needed to keep the cost acceptable.

The stated epsilon holds only if the code matches the accountant's assumptions. The usual accountants assume each batch is drawn by including every example independently at random, but many pipelines shuffle the data and cut it into fixed batches; an audit of models trained that way measured privacy loss up to four times the epsilon they reported. A claim should name the sampling method and accountant, and differential privacy auditing can test the figure empirically.

The guarantee protects one training example, not one person. If a patient has ten admissions or a customer hundreds of messages in the training set, their protection is much weaker than epsilon suggests, because the bound loosens with the number of examples they contribute. Capping each person's contribution, or making each person a single example, gives a guarantee at the level of the person, at some cost in data and accuracy.

No agreed value of epsilon makes a model private, and large values are common: the method's original headline results used epsilon 8, at which a training outcome may be about 3,000 times more likely with a given example than without it, and the Opacus image tutorial targets 50. Hyperparameter searches run on the private data also leak information unless their cost is added to the budget. A claim should state epsilon, delta, the unit of privacy and what the budget covers.

Computing a separate gradient for every example costs memory and time; in the original experiments one training epoch went from about 40 to about 180 seconds. Layers that combine examples within a batch, such as batch normalisation, break the per-example bound and must be replaced, for example with group normalisation, so an existing architecture may need changing and re-tuning before it can be trained privately.
